The same result follows from a derivation in vector notation,
which treats $(b_0, b_1)$ as a single vector
instead of differentiating with respect to each component separately.

::: proof

Collect the coefficients and each observation's covariates into vectors:

$$
\v{b} \eqdef \begin{pmatrix} b_0 \\ b_1 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\vxi \eqdef \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ x_i \end{pmatrix},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
b_0 + b_1 x_i = \tprod{\vxi}{\v{b}}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\text{RSS}(\v{b}) = \sumin \paren{y_i - \tprod{\vxi}{\v{b}}}^2.
$$

**Gradient.**
For any constant vector $\v{a}$,
$\deriv{\v{b}} \tprod{\v{a}}{\v{b}} = \v{a}$,
since the $j$th component of $\tprod{\v{a}}{\v{b}}$'s gradient is
$\deriv{b_j} \sum_k a_k b_k = a_j$.
So:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\deriv{\v{b}} \text{RSS}(\v{b})
&= \sumin 2 \paren{y_i - \tprod{\vxi}{\v{b}}}
  \deriv{\v{b}} \paren{y_i - \tprod{\vxi}{\v{b}}}
&& \text{(chain rule, term by term)}\\
&= -2 \sumin \vxi \paren{y_i - \tprod{\vxi}{\v{b}}}
&& \text{($\deriv{\v{b}} \tprod{\vxi}{\v{b}} = \vxi$)}\\
&= -2 \paren{\sumin \vxi y_i - \sumin \vxi \tprod{\vxi}{\v{b}}}
&& \text{(distribute the sum)}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Solve for $\hat{\v{b}}$.**
Write $A \eqdef \sumin \soprod{\vxi}$ and $\v{c} \eqdef \sumin \vxi y_i$,
so that the gradient is $-2 \paren{\v{c} - A \v{b}}$.
Setting it equal to $\vzero$ gives the
**normal equations** $A \v{b} = \v{c}$.
Writing out the components of each term:

$$
A = \sumin \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x_i \\ x_i & x_i^2 \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} n & n\bar{x} \\ n\bar{x} & \sumin x_i^2 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\v{c} = \sumin \begin{pmatrix} y_i \\ x_i y_i \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} n\bar{y} \\ \sumin x_i y_i \end{pmatrix}.
$$

The determinant of $A$ is
$n \sumin x_i^2 - n^2 \bar{x}^2 = n S_{xx} > 0$,
so $A$ is invertible and the normal equations have the unique solution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\v{b}} = A^{-1} \v{c}
&= \frac{1}{n S_{xx}}
  \begin{pmatrix} \sumin x_i^2 & -n\bar{x} \\ -n\bar{x} & n \end{pmatrix}
  \begin{pmatrix} n\bar{y} \\ \sumin x_i y_i \end{pmatrix}
&& \text{(inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix)}\\
&= \frac{1}{S_{xx}}
  \begin{pmatrix}
  \bar{y} \sumin x_i^2 - \bar{x} \sumin x_i y_i \\
  \sumin x_i y_i - n \bar{x} \bar{y}
  \end{pmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply, cancel $n$)}\\
&= \frac{1}{S_{xx}}
  \begin{pmatrix}
  \bar{y} \paren{S_{xx} + n\bar{x}^2} - \bar{x} \paren{S_{xy} + n\bar{x}\bar{y}} \\
  S_{xy}
  \end{pmatrix}
&& \text{($\sumin x_i^2 = S_{xx} + n\bar{x}^2$, $\sumin x_i y_i = S_{xy} + n\bar{x}\bar{y}$)}\\
&= \begin{pmatrix}
  \bar{y} - \bar{x} \, S_{xy} / S_{xx} \\
  S_{xy} / S_{xx}
  \end{pmatrix}
&& \text{(cancel $\pm n\bar{x}^2\bar{y}$)}
\end{aligned}
$$

which matches $\hat\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \hat\beta_1 \bar{x}$
and $\hat\beta_1 = S_{xy} / S_{xx}$.

**Second derivative.**
Differentiating the gradient $-2 \paren{\v{c} - A \v{b}}$
with respect to $\tp{\v{b}}$ gives the
[Hessian](intro-MLEs.qmd#def-hessian) of $\text{RSS}$:

$$
\deriv{\v{b}} \deriv{\tp{\v{b}}} \text{RSS}(\v{b})
= 2 A
= 2 \sumin \soprod{\vxi}.
$$

It is positive definite.
For any vector $\v{v} = \tp{(v_0, v_1)} \neq \vzero$:

$$
\tp{\v{v}} \paren{2 A} \v{v}
= 2 \sumin \tprod{\v{v}}{\vxi} \tprod{\vxi}{\v{v}}
= 2 \sumin \paren{v_0 + v_1 x_i}^2
\ge 0,
$$

with equality only if $v_0 + v_1 x_i = 0$ for every $i$.
If $v_1 \neq 0$, that would force every $x_i = -v_0 / v_1$,
contradicting $S_{xx} > 0$;
if $v_1 = 0$, it would force $v_0 = 0$,
contradicting $\v{v} \neq \vzero$.
So the inequality is strict,
the Hessian is positive definite at every $\v{b}$,
$\text{RSS}$ is strictly convex,
and $\hat{\v{b}}$ is its unique global minimum.

:::
